title: Fire Shelter Testing
description: David Maclay Schulte, an equipment specialist at T and D, emphasizes the importance of evaluating and reassessing training for fire shelter. He discusses the significance of maintaining specifications and standards for fire shelter, as well as the assessment of accident sites, deployment situations, and firefighters' injuries. The in-house production of training materials and the use of prototypes for field testing are highlighted, along with the collaboration with engineering and videography departments for continuous improvement and innovation.

transcript.text: There's a lot of moving parts in the
fire shelter . It's just an aluminized
tent , but there's a lot that goes into
it . My name is David McClay Schulte .
I'm an equipment specialist here at T&D .
A fire shelter is an illuminized single
occupancy cloth tent that is used to
protect the firefighter against radiant
heat . My role is to maintain the
specifications and the standards and
keep evaluating and reassessing the
training for the fire shelter to make
sure that we are still providing the
best that we can provide to the
firefighters . Specifications are very
important because that's what you use
to make certain you're getting what you
want . And when it comes to the fire
shelter , there's a lot that goes into
it . We go to these accident sites and
we evaluate the situation that they
went through . Deployment site itself .
What's the vegetation like , how far is
it from where they deployed their
shelter to what was burning , and then
of course we evaluate the fire shelter
itself to see what kind of thermal
damage was done to that , what kind of
signs . are present . We also evaluate
the firefighters themselves . Did they
receive any burn injuries ? And if so ,
where ? And then their personal
protective equipment , their shirts ,
their pants , their gloves , their
helmet . We evaluate all of that
because there's indicators for certain
levels of heat , certain temperatures
that you can see on personal protective
equipment . Well , a large part of the
fire shelter program isn't just the
fire shelter itself , it's all of the
training that is associated with it . A
lot of our products that come out ,
whether it's a video product like the
fire shelter training video , that's
all done in-house here . Even our
printed work is done by the in-house
photographers . It's a combined effort
to always be looking for the next best
thing so that we can come up with the
best possible product for those on the
ground . We were doing the life cycle
evaluation , we had prototypes that
went into the field for actual field
testing . We worked with the shop down
here , and they built us forms and we
were able to use our own ovens and
create our own liners to keep the
shelters better protected for the
prototype study . We use a lot of the
engineering folk in here because of
their experience with thermocouples .
Then the videography department is
hugely important because we have video
cameras set up inside and outside the
shelter , so we see what's going on and
all of that . When you go to a
deployment and you talk to the people
who went through it because they
survived , because the shelter allowed
them to go home to their family to
continue living , that's very rewarding .
It makes it absolutely all worthwhile ,
and it really drives me to want to find
better components and materials for the
fire shelter so that people can go home
to their families after more and more
intense burnovers .
